title: Ballpoint pens? Heck yes, ballpoint pens!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the ballpoint pen, starting with a playful debate over pen colors and a tour of writing history: cave carvings, Chinese Indian ink, Tien Chew's colored inks, the Roman reed pen, and the quill pen that lasted about a thousand years. They cover fountain pens and why they flood at high altitude, then the ballpoint's invention: the 1800s idea, Laszlo Biro's fast-drying ink and patent with his brother George, the Royal Air Force order, Milton Reynolds' knockoff, Gimbels' sales, and Marcel Bic's cheap disposable pen. They explain the ball-and-socket mechanism (compared to roll-on deodorant), ink composition (pigments, dyes, vehicles, tannins, additives), why ballpoints fail upside down, and the Fisher Space Pen versus the space-pencil legend. They also discuss erasable pens, rollerball pens, and restaurant check presenters. The episode closes with listener mail about Colorado fourteeners and search and rescue costs.
topics: Colorado fourteeners search and rescue listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and pen color debate
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on ballpoint pens and banter about favorite pen colors and inks for marking printed notes.

segments.title: History of writing, ink, and early pens
segments.summary: From cave carvings and Greek wax tablets to Chinese Indian ink, Tien Chew's colored inks, the Roman reed pen, and the quill pen, which was the dominant writing tool for about a thousand years.

segments.title: Fountain pens and the altitude problem
segments.summary: The hosts discuss fountain pens and their enthusiast subculture, then explain why fountain pens flood in airplanes because trapped air expands as pressure drops, pushing ink out.

segments.title: Invention of the ballpoint by Biro
segments.summary: The idea dates to the 1800s, but it was László Bíró, a Hungarian journalist, who with his chemist brother George developed fast-drying ink and a ballpoint patent. The Royal Air Force bought large numbers, and Bíró founded the Bureau Pen Company.

segments.title: Reynolds, Gimbels, and the patent fights
segments.summary: Milton Reynolds copied the Biro design and sold Reynolds pens at Gimbels for $12.50. Patent lawsuits went nowhere, and early Reynolds pens were recalled over defects. Bic later made cheap disposable ballpoints.

segments.title: How a ballpoint works and the roll-on deodorant comparison
segments.summary: The hosts describe the tiny ball held in a socket that keeps ink from spilling, rolls ink onto paper, and is compared to roll-on deodorant. They also discuss tip sizes such as the 0.7 mm Pilot G2.

segments.title: Ballpoint ink composition and why pens fail upside down
segments.summary: Ink is made of pigment or dye in a vehicle, with additives like gum arabic. Tannins are discussed as possibly a vehicle or additive, with uncertainty. Ink must be thick enough to hold but flow under gravity, which is why ballpoints fail when written upside down.

segments.title: Space pens, the space pencil myth, and erasable pens
segments.summary: The Fisher Space Pen used pressurized ink to write in zero gravity and upside down. The hosts say the space pencil legend is mostly false, though NASA did buy mechanical pencils. They also cover the 1980s erasable pen that used rubber cement ink, and rollerball pens.

segments.title: Writing surfaces and restaurant check presenters
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh talk about how paper and surfaces affect the writing experience, plus restaurant check folders.

segments.title: Listener mail: Colorado fourteeners and search and rescue
segments.summary: A listener named Tyler Nesbar writes about Colorado's fourteeners, rising population, the debate over charging for search and rescue, and the dangers of Capitol Peak.
